meta_title: Partial Fractions Integration: NCERT Exemplar Q38
meta_desc: Solve NCERT Exemplar Class 12 Q38: integrate (2x-1)/[(x-1)(x+2)(x-3)] by partial fractions, step by step. Try the free 8-question quiz to lock it in.

quiz.title: Partial Fractions Integration Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on splitting a rational function over distinct linear factors and integrating to logarithms. Pick an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Integration by partial fractions over distinct linear factors

questions.q: To decompose (2x-1)/[(x-1)(x+2)(x-3)], which form is correct?
questions.explanation: Each factor is distinct and linear, so each contributes a single constant over that factor: A/(x-1) + B/(x+2) + C/(x-3).

questions.q: Using the cover-up method, what is A (the coefficient of 1/(x-1))?
questions.explanation: Cover (x-1) and put x=1 in the rest: (2·1-1)/[(1+2)(1-3)] = 1/[3·(-2)] = -1/6. So A = -1/6.

questions.q: By cover-up, the constant over (x+2) is found by substituting which value of x?
questions.explanation: The factor (x+2) is zero when x = -2, so you cover it and evaluate the rest at x = -2.

questions.q: The integral of A/(x-1) with respect to x is:
questions.explanation: ∫ A/(x-1) dx = A ln|x-1| + C, since the derivative of ln|x-1| is 1/(x-1).

questions.q: Cover-up for a factor (x-a) works because at x=a the other partial-fraction terms:
options: vanish, since each is multiplied by (x-a)
questions.explanation: After multiplying through by (x-a), every other term still carries a factor (x-a), which is zero at x=a, leaving only that term's constant.

questions.q: The constant over (x-3), by cover-up, is (2·3-1)/[(3-1)(3+2)]. This equals:
questions.explanation: Numerator 5, denominator (2)(5)=10, so 5/10 = 1/2. The constant over (x-3) is 1/2.

questions.q: After decomposing, the full integral is a sum of terms each of the form:
questions.explanation: Each 1/(x-a) integrates to ln|x-a|, so the answer is a linear combination of logarithms plus a constant.

questions.q: Why must every constant (A, B, C) be checked for consistency, e.g. by comparing coefficients?
options: To confirm the decomposition reproduces the original numerator
questions.explanation: Recombining A/(x-1)+B/(x+2)+C/(x-3) must give back (2x-1)/[(x-1)(x+2)(x-3)]; comparing numerators confirms the constants are right.

faq.q: When can I use partial fractions to integrate a rational function?
faq.a: Use partial fractions when the integrand is a ratio of polynomials and the denominator factorises. First make sure the degree of the numerator is less than the degree of the denominator; if not, do polynomial long division first, then split the proper fraction into simpler pieces.

faq.q: What is the cover-up method and when does it work?
faq.a: The cover-up (Heaviside) method finds the constant over a distinct linear factor (x-a) quickly: cover that factor and substitute x=a into everything else. It works only for non-repeated linear factors. Repeated or quadratic factors need the full coefficient-comparison approach.

faq.q: Why do the answers come out as natural logarithms?
faq.a: Each simple term 1/(x-a) integrates to ln|x-a|, because the derivative of ln|x-a| is 1/(x-a). So a fraction over distinct linear factors always integrates to a sum of logarithm terms plus a constant of integration.

faq.q: Do I always need the absolute value signs inside the log?
faq.a: Yes, keep |x-a| inside the logarithm. The argument of ln can be negative for some x values in the domain, and the absolute value keeps the antiderivative valid on both sides of x=a.
